items.skill_note: Satisfaction and price say nothing about whether exercise increased.

items.passage: An entomologist claims that a neonicotinoid seed treatment is responsible for the decline of wild bee colonies on farms where it is used.
items.stem:
Colony losses on treated and untreated farms appear in the table.

Farm type | Colony loss over 3 years (%)
---|---
Treated fields | 22
Untreated fields | 21

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the entomologist's claim?
choices: Treated seeds are coated at a rate of 0.5 milligrams per seed.
Losses were 22% on treated farms and 21% on untreated farms, a gap of 1 percentage points.
Wild bee species differ in their foraging range.
Wild bee species nest in the same hedgerows on both farm types.
items.explanation: Nearly identical losses with and without the treatment leave the pesticide unable to explain the decline.
items.skill_note: A dose rate describes exposure, not effect; the comparison is what matters.

items.passage: Fisheries biologists propose that a newly installed fish ladder will let adult salmon reach their spawning grounds above the dam.
items.stem:
The ladder opened in 2021; counts appear in the table.

Year | Salmon counted above the dam
---|---
2019 (before) | 40
2023 (after) | 960

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the proposal?
choices: Water temperature above the dam is two degrees cooler than below.
The ladder's design was adapted from a similar structure in Norway.
Counts above the dam rose from 40 to 960 after the ladder opened, while counts at the dam's base were unchanged.
The ladder cost 4.2 million dollars and took three years to build.
items.explanation: A twentyfold increase above the dam with no change below is what passage through the ladder would produce.
items.skill_note: Cost and temperature do not show that fish passed.

items.passage: An archaeologist argues that glass beads found at an inland settlement arrived through long-distance trade rather than being made locally.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?
choices: The beads were found in graves alongside imported pottery.
The settlement lay on a river navigable for six months of the year.
Similar beads have been recovered from three other inland sites.
The beads' trace-element signature matches a workshop on the coast 2,000 kilometers away, and no glass-making debris has been found at the inland site in forty years of excavation.
items.explanation: A chemical match to a distant workshop plus the total absence of production debris establishes import.
items.skill_note: A navigable river shows transport was possible, not that these beads were transported.

items.passage: A wildlife agency argues that a native bird's decline on an island began with the arrival of a introduced predator in 1994.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the agency's argument?
choices: Museum specimens and survey notes show the bird's numbers had fallen by half between 1960 and 1990, four decades before the predator was recorded.
The predator was first recorded near the island's main harbor.
The predator's diet includes the bird's eggs.
Two other native birds on the island have stable populations.
items.explanation: A decline that predates the predator cannot have been caused by it.
items.skill_note: A plausible diet explains how predation could matter, not when the decline started.

items.passage: An advertising agency reports that its summer campaign increased sales of a soft drink, noting that sales rose fourteen percent during the campaign.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the agency's claim?
choices: The campaign cost three million dollars and ran for six weeks.
The drink's main competitor also ran advertisements that summer.
Sales of the diet version rose more slowly than the regular version.
Sales in the four regions where the campaign did not run rose by the same fourteen percent over the same weeks, during a heat wave.
items.explanation: An equal rise where no advertising ran attributes the increase to the heat wave rather than the campaign.
items.skill_note: A competitor's advertising would muddy the picture but does not isolate the campaign's effect.

items.passage: A soil conservation team argues that planting a winter cover crop between rows of corn reduces erosion on sloping fields, because the roots hold the soil through the spring rains.
items.stem:
The trial ran on eight sloping fields of the same soil type.

Field treatment | Soil lost over one spring (t/ha)
---|---
Bare between rows | 4.1
Cover cropped | 1.2

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's argument?
choices: Cover-cropped fields lost 1.2  t/ha against 4.1  t/ha on bare fields, a reduction of about 2.9  t/ha.
Cover crop seed cost forty dollars per hectare.
Cover-cropped fields held slightly more earthworms per square meter.
The cover crop was killed before the corn was planted.
items.explanation: The claim is about erosion, and a 2.9 t/ha reduction on matched fields is a direct measurement of it.
items.skill_note: Earthworm counts and seed costs are side observations; erosion is the outcome named in the claim.

items.passage: A maritime archaeologist argues that a wreck found off the coast sank in the early seventeenth century rather than the eighteenth, as local tradition holds.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?
choices: The ship carried a cargo of iron cannon of a common design.
Eleven coins recovered from beneath the hull were minted between 1602 and 1611, and the ship's fasteners are of a type replaced by another pattern after 1620.
The wreck lies in twelve meters of water near a busy shipping lane.
Local fishermen have avoided the site for generations.
items.explanation: Dated coins establish a terminus after 1611, and fasteners abandoned after 1620 establish a terminus before it.
items.skill_note: A common cannon design spans both centuries and cannot discriminate between them.

items.passage: A public health department reports that its tax on sugary drinks cut consumption in the city by eighteen percent and credits the tax.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the department's claim?
choices: The tax raised eleven million dollars in its first year.
Bottlers reduced the sugar content of two products voluntarily.
Consumption fell by nineteen percent over the same period in a neighboring city with no such tax, after a national advertising campaign against sugar.
Retailers near the city border reported increased sales.
items.explanation: An equal decline without the tax attributes the drop to the national campaign rather than the local policy.
items.skill_note: Border shopping may shift where drinks are bought, but it does not explain the size of the citywide decline.

items.passage: A pharmacist hypothesizes that a once-daily formulation will improve adherence compared with the twice-daily version of the same drug, mainly by removing the midday dose that patients most often forget.
items.stem:
Adherence was measured by electronic pill-bottle caps over six months.

Formulation | Patients taking at least 80% of doses (%)
---|---
Twice daily | 71
Once daily | 88

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?
choices: Both versions contain the same total monthly dose.
The once-daily version costs eleven percent more per month.
88% of patients on the once-daily version reached the adherence threshold, against 71% on the twice-daily version.
Both versions were supplied by the same manufacturer.
items.explanation: The hypothesis concerns adherence, and the seventeen-point gap on an objective measure is direct support.
items.skill_note: Cost and supply arrangements describe the products, not whether patients took them.

items.passage: A district administrator argues that a new writing curriculum, introduced in 2019, raised eighth-grade writing scores, which rose by twelve points between 2020 and 2023.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the administrator's argument?
choices: The curriculum was developed by a team of twelve teachers.
Teachers attended monthly workshops during the first year.
The curriculum was piloted in four schools before adoption.
The scores had already risen by eleven points between 2016 and 2019, before any teacher received the new materials, and the upward trend continued at the same slope afterward.
items.explanation: A trend of the same slope before and after adoption leaves nothing for the curriculum to explain.
items.skill_note: Piloting shows the program was tested; it does not separate the program from the existing trend.

items.passage: A transportation planner argues that installing protected bike lanes reduced cyclist injuries on a corridor, because the lanes separate riders from moving traffic.
items.stem:
The lanes were installed in 2021; rates appear in the table.

Period | Injuries per million km cycled
---|---
2018-2020 | 2.8
2022-2024 | 1.1

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the planner's argument?
choices: Injury rates fell from 2.8 to 1.1 per million kilometers after installation, while cycling volumes on the corridor rose by a third.
Cyclists surveyed said they felt safer in the lanes.
The lanes cost 1.8 million dollars per kilometer.
Two intersections along the corridor were rebuilt at the same time.
items.explanation: A 60 percent drop in injuries while exposure rose is strong evidence that separation, not reduced riding, produced the change.
items.skill_note: Feeling safer is a perception; the rate per kilometer is the outcome that matters.

items.passage: A conservation agency claims that removing introduced rats from four seabird islands between 2010 and 2015 increased the islands' breeding seabird populations.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Seabird chicks are vulnerable to rat predation in the nest.
Seabird counts rose by a similar margin on three comparable islands where rats were never present and no removal was attempted.
Two of the treated islands are nature reserves.
Rat removal was carried out with poisoned bait spread by helicopter.
items.explanation: A comparable rise on islands with no rats and no intervention points to a regional cause rather than the removal.
items.skill_note: Vulnerability to predation explains why rats could matter; it does not show that removal caused the increase.

items.passage: A charity reports that its spring advertising campaign increased donations, noting that donations rose thirty percent during the eight weeks the campaign ran.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the charity's claim?
choices: Donations to comparable charities that ran no advertising rose by thirty-one percent over the same eight weeks, following a widely reported disaster abroad.
The campaign cost 90,000 dollars and ran on radio and social media.
Donations fell sharply in the two months after the campaign ended.
The charity's donor base had grown slowly for three years.
items.explanation: An equal rise across charities without advertising attributes the increase to the disaster coverage.
items.skill_note: A post-campaign fall is consistent with either explanation and does not isolate the advertising.

items.passage: A wetland restoration team claims that reflooding a marsh drained in the 1950s increased its use by migratory waterfowl, which stop there each spring.
items.stem:
Reflooding was completed in 2021; peak spring counts appear in the table.

Year | Peak waterfowl count (birds)
---|---
2019 | 45
2024 | 118

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim?
choices: The restoration cost 3.1 million dollars and took four years.
Water clarity improved measurably after reflooding.
Peak counts rose from 45 to 118 birds after reflooding, with most of the increase in diving ducks that feed in open water.
Two other marshes in the region were restored in the same period.
items.explanation: A 2.6-fold increase concentrated in species that require open water is direct evidence that reflooding created usable habitat.
items.skill_note: Improved clarity is a physical side effect; the claim is about bird numbers.

items.passage: An archaeologist argues that obsidian tools found at an inland village were imported from a source 300 kilometers away rather than gathered locally.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Obsidian tools were found in three houses at the site.
Trace-element analysis of the tools matches the fingerprint of a specific obsidian flow on the coast, and no obsidian source exists within 200 kilometers of the village.
The village lies on a river that flows to the coast.
The tools show wear consistent with harvesting grain.
items.explanation: A chemical match to a distant flow, plus the absence of any local source, establishes transport.
items.skill_note: A river route shows transport was feasible, not that it happened.

items.passage: A psychologist claims that a computerized memory training program improves everyday memory in older adults, citing gains on the program's own tasks.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Participants enjoyed the program and completed most sessions.
The program was tested in four countries.
Younger adults improved faster than older adults on the trained tasks.

Participants improved steadily on the trained tasks but showed no improvement on independent tests of remembering names and appointments, and a control group playing crossword puzzles gained as much on those tests.
items.explanation: Improvement confined to the trained task, with no transfer and an equally improving control, undercuts a claim about everyday memory.
items.skill_note: Enjoyment and completion show the program was usable, not effective.

items.passage: A dental researcher claims that water fluoridation, adopted by a city in 2011, reduced cavities among children there, compared with a nearby city that never fluoridated.
items.stem:
Both cities are in the same region and have similar incomes.

City | Mean decayed teeth per child
---|---
Fluoridated since 2011 | 1.9
Never fluoridated | 1.8

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Children in the fluoridated city averaged 1.9 decayed teeth against 1.8 in the never-fluoridated city.
Both cities ran school brushing programs.
The fluoridated city added fluoride at 0.7 milligrams per liter.
Cavity rates in the region have fallen since 1990.
items.explanation: A slightly worse outcome in the fluoridated city than in a comparable unfluoridated one directly contradicts the claim.
items.skill_note: School brushing programs in both cities would make the comparison fairer, not weaker.

items.passage: A housing agency argues that adding cavity-wall insulation to its older properties lowered the energy needed to heat them, and that the saving would repay the cost within a decade.
items.stem:
Insulated and uninsulated properties of the same age and construction appear in the table.

Property group | Mean annual heating energy (kWh)
---|---
Uninsulated | 14200
Insulated | 9100

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the agency's argument?
choices: Residents reported that their homes felt warmer in winter.
The insulation was installed by three contractors over two years.
The agency owns 4,100 properties built between 1930 and 1955.
Insulated properties used 9100  kWh a year against 14200  kWh for comparable uninsulated ones, a saving of about 5100  kWh.
items.explanation: A 5,100 kWh annual saving on matched properties, at prevailing prices, is the quantity that determines whether the cost is repaid within a decade.
items.skill_note: Feeling warmer is subjective; only the metered saving supports a payback claim.

items.passage: A museum reports that extending its opening hours to 9 p.m. on Thursdays increased attendance by a quarter, and credits the new schedule.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the museum's claim?
choices: The museum's annual report was published in September.
Attendance rose by a similar amount at four other museums in the same city that kept their old hours, during a summer when a new transit line opened nearby.
The extended hours required hiring six additional gallery attendants.
The museum's cafe stayed open later on Thursdays.
items.explanation: A comparable rise at museums that did not change their hours points to the transit line rather than the schedule.
items.skill_note: Extra staffing and cafe hours describe how the change was delivered.

items.passage: An ecologist claims that a widely used insecticide is responsible for declines in frog populations on farmland ponds, where the chemical is applied to crops each spring.
items.stem:
Ponds on treated and untreated farms appear in the table.

Pond type | Decline in frog numbers over 5 years (%)
---|---
Treated farms | 46
Untreated farms | 44

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Frog tadpoles are known to be sensitive to many chemicals.
The insecticide is applied to cereal crops in spring.
Frogs declined 46% on treated farms and 44% on untreated farms, a difference of 2 points.
Treated farms used about 1.2 kilograms per hectare.
items.explanation: Nearly identical declines with and without the insecticide leave it unable to explain the pattern.
items.skill_note: Tadpole sensitivity describes a possible mechanism, not an observed effect.

items.passage: A company claims its vocabulary app increased users' working vocabulary, citing a gain of 300 words among users who completed a twelve-week course.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the company's claim?
choices: Users who completed the course scored higher than non-users before starting it, and their scores rose no more than those of a comparison group that read novels for the same twelve weeks.
Users could choose among four topic areas.
The course required about fifteen minutes a day.
The app's subscription fee was waived for students.
items.explanation: A pre-existing advantage plus no gain over an active comparison group means the app cannot claim the improvement.
items.skill_note: Daily time commitment shows the course was substantial, not that it worked.

items.passage: A water utility argues that switching from chloramine to chlorine disinfection reduced gastrointestinal illness in its service area, despite an increase in taste complaints.
items.stem:
The switch occurred in March; case rates appear in the table.

Period | Reported cases per 100,000 residents
---|---
Year before switch | 31
Year after switch | 12

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the utility's argument?
choices: Taste complaints rose by 400 percent after the switch.
Reported cases fell from 31 to 12 per 100,000 residents, while monitoring showed chlorine residuals maintained throughout the distribution system.
Chlorine costs less per liter than chloramine.
items.explanation: A 60 percent drop in reported illness, with residuals confirming the disinfectant reached the system, supports the claim.
items.skill_note: Taste complaints and cost are real consequences that do not bear on whether illness fell.

items.passage: A state credits its 2016 rooftop solar subsidy, which covered a quarter of installation costs, with a tripling of residential installations between 2016 and 2020.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the state's claim?
choices: Installations were concentrated in the wealthiest counties.
The state's utilities raised retail electricity rates in 2017.
The subsidy covered 25 percent of installation costs.
Installations tripled over the same four years in four neighboring states that offered no subsidy, as panel prices fell by half nationally.
items.explanation: The same tripling without any subsidy, coinciding with a national price collapse, removes the policy as the explanation.
items.skill_note: Higher electricity rates could increase demand anywhere; they do not separate the subsidy's effect.

items.passage: A film commission credits the state's 2015 tax incentive, worth about eighteen cents per dollar of qualified spending, with a doubling of location shooting days.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the commission's claim?
choices: Two large productions used the incentive in its first year.
Shooting days doubled over the same period in three neighboring states without incentives, following the national release of a cheaper camera system that made location work affordable.
The incentive returned about 18 cents per dollar of qualified spending.
The state's filming permits are issued by county offices.
items.explanation: The same doubling without incentives, tied to a national technology change, leaves the tax policy unable to explain it.
items.skill_note: Two productions using the incentive shows take-up, not a state-wide effect.

items.passage: An ornithologist claims that urban noise has driven birds in a city to sing at a higher pitch than birds of the same species in nearby rural areas.
items.stem:
Recordings from city and rural sites appear in the table.

Location | Mean song frequency (kHz)
---|---
City center | 3.4
Rural sites | 3.3

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: City birds sang at 3.4  kHz and rural birds at 3.3  kHz, a difference of 0.1  kHz.
City noise levels were 18 decibels higher than rural levels.
The species is abundant in both habitats.
Recordings were made at dawn during the breeding season.
items.explanation: A 0.1 kHz difference is negligible, so the data provide no support for a noise-driven pitch shift.
items.skill_note: Higher noise confirms the exposure but not the claimed response.

items.passage: An archaeologist argues that a large ceramic vessel found in a Bronze Age house was used to store olive oil rather than grain.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The vessel could hold about 200 liters.
The vessel was found in a room containing three grinding stones.
Similar vessels appear at sites along the coast.
Residue absorbed into the vessel's fabric contains high concentrations of oleic acid and the waxes found in olive oil, with no starch granules anywhere on the interior.
items.explanation: Absorbed lipid residues identify the contents directly, and the absence of starch excludes grain.
items.skill_note: Capacity and coastal parallels say nothing about what was inside.

items.passage: A coastal agency claims that planting belts of mangrove along the shore reduced storm damage to the villages behind them during a 2022 cyclone.
items.stem:
Damage was assessed on a 0-100 index after a storm of uniform strength.

Village shoreline | Mean structural damage after the 2022 storm (index score)
---|---
No mangrove belt | 62
Mangrove belt | 24

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the claim?
choices: The agency intends to extend planting to two more districts.
The mangrove species used grows about a meter a year.
Villages behind a mangrove belt scored 24 on the damage index against 62 where no belt existed, at comparable exposure and elevation.
Planting was carried out by village volunteers.
items.explanation: A 38-point damage difference at comparable exposure and elevation is a direct measure of protection.
items.skill_note: Growth rate and labor describe the planting, not its protective effect.

items.passage: A supplement company claims that magnesium tablets reduce night-time leg cramps in adults over sixty, a group that reports cramps more often than any other.
items.stem:
Participants were randomized to magnesium or placebo for twelve weeks.

Group | Cramp nights per month
---|---
Placebo | 6.2
Magnesium | 6

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Blood magnesium rose measurably in the supplement group.
Magnesium users reported 6 cramp nights a month against 6.2 on placebo, a difference of 0.2 nights.
Participants were recruited from six clinics.
Cramps are more common in people over sixty-five.
items.explanation: A 0.2-night difference is trivial next to a baseline of six, so the data do not support a benefit.
items.skill_note: Rising blood levels show absorption, not effect.

items.passage: A city argues that replacing its streetlights with brighter LEDs at a hundred intersections reduced night-time crashes there, mostly by making pedestrians visible sooner.
items.stem:
Treated and untreated intersections matched on traffic volume appear in the table.

Intersection group | Night-time crashes per year
---|---
Unchanged lighting | 9.1
LED lighting | 4.2

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Treated intersections recorded 4.2 night-time crashes a year against 9.1 at matched intersections with unchanged lighting.
The conversion was completed over eighteen months.
The LEDs consume 60 percent less electricity than the old fixtures.
Residents reported that the streets felt safer at night.
items.explanation: A halving of night-time crashes at matched intersections is the outcome the claim requires.
items.skill_note: Energy savings and perceived safety are separate benefits; neither measures crashes.

items.passage: A retailer claims that its 2021 sales training program, a two-day course for branch staff, increased sales per employee across the company's 240 stores.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The company spent 300,000 dollars on the program.
Trained branches reported higher employee satisfaction.
The program ran for two days and included role-play exercises.
Sales per employee rose by the same percentage in the company's branches that did not receive the training, during a year when a competitor closed nine stores nearby.
items.explanation: An equal rise in untrained branches points to the competitor's closures rather than the training.
items.skill_note: Satisfaction is a different outcome from sales, and it does not establish a sales effect.

items.passage: After a district moved its high school start time from 7:30 to 8:45, average scores on the state test rose by eleven points. Administrators concluded that the later start had raised achievement by allowing students to sleep longer.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the administrators' conclusion?
choices: Some students said they preferred the later start time.
Neighboring districts that kept early start times also saw scores rise slightly.
Students reported sleeping the same number of hours as before, and the score gain appeared only in classes that had also received a new teacher.
The district's scores had been below the state average for a decade.
items.explanation: If sleep did not change and the gain is confined to classes with a new teacher, the sleep explanation loses its mechanism and its scope.
items.skill_note: Look for the finding that removes the causal link, not one that merely adds background.

items.passage: Excavations at a lowland Maya city show that construction stopped and the population dispersed within about fifty years around 900 CE. A historian argues that a prolonged drought, rather than warfare, ended the city.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
choices: Stone tools from the site show no signs of battle damage.
A sediment core from the city's reservoir records the region's driest half-century in two millennia during exactly that period, while a nearby city with a spring-fed canal system continued to build.
The city's last inscribed monument dates to 909 CE.
Drought is known to have affected several regions of Mesoamerica in the ninth century.
items.explanation: A drought precisely coinciding with abandonment, plus survival of a city with an independent water source, isolates water as the decisive difference.
items.skill_note: Absence of battle damage is consistent with drought but does not distinguish it from other peaceful causes.

items.passage: A sleep laboratory hypothesizes that losing ninety minutes of sleep per night impairs reaction time more than it impairs accuracy on a simple visual task.
items.stem:
Participants were randomized to normal sleep or a 90-minute reduction for two weeks.

Group | Change in reaction time (ms)
---|---
Normal sleep | 4
Restricted sleep | 38

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the hypothesis?
choices: Restricted participants reported feeling sleepier on a standard questionnaire.
Reaction time slowed by 38  ms in the restricted group but by only 4  ms in the normal group, while accuracy was unchanged in both.
Accuracy fell by two percentage points in the restricted group.
The laboratory kept room temperature at 21 degrees for both groups.
items.explanation: The hypothesis makes a comparative claim about reaction time versus accuracy; the table shows a large reaction-time cost with accuracy intact.
items.skill_note: Feeling sleepy is a subjective report, not a performance measure.

items.passage: A state senator argues that raising the minimum wage to fifteen dollars caused the restaurant job losses recorded in her state the following year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the senator's argument?
choices: The state's overall unemployment rate was unchanged.
The minimum wage increase passed by a narrow margin.
Restaurant employment in bordering counties of a neighboring state that kept its lower minimum wage fell by the same percentage over the same year.
Several restaurant owners said they had reduced hours after the increase.
items.explanation: An identical decline where no increase occurred removes the policy as the explanation and points to a regional cause.
items.skill_note: Owner complaints and a stable overall rate do not separate the policy from other shocks; a comparison group does.

items.passage: Conservators argue that the museum's east gallery needs a dehumidifier rather than a heater, because the damage to the wooden panels is caused by repeated cycles of moisture absorption rather than by low temperature.
items.stem:
Both galleries are kept at the same average temperature.

Gallery | Mean daily humidity swing (%)
---|---
East (panels cracked) | 18
West (panels intact) | 4

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the conservators' argument?
choices: The east gallery's humidity swings by 18% a day against 4% in the west, where panels of the same wood and age are intact.
Visitors spend more time in the east gallery on weekends.
The east gallery's average temperature is one degree lower than the west's.
The east gallery's panels were acquired from a different donor.
items.explanation: The claim is about moisture cycling as the cause of damage; matched panels differing in humidity swing but not temperature isolate that variable.
items.skill_note: A one-degree temperature difference would support a competing explanation, not the conservators'.

items.passage: A materials scientist argues that a portrait could not have been painted before 1870, because its blue pigment contains a compound first synthesized in that decade.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the scientist's argument?
choices: The portrait's canvas was woven in France in the 1860s.
The artist's signature was added by a later hand.
The portrait was first catalogued in 1912.
The pigment's signature trace elements match the original 1871 manufacturing process, and no sample from a securely dated pre-1870 painting contains the compound.
items.explanation: Matching the 1871 process, plus absence from securely dated earlier works, fixes the pigment's earliest possible use.
items.skill_note: An 1860s canvas only sets a lower bound for the support, not for the paint.

items.passage: A hospital's infectious-disease team claims that a new cleaning protocol, introduced across its surgical wards in July, reduced the number of infections following operations.
items.stem:
The protocol was introduced in July; rates for the two half-years appear in the table.

Period | Infections per 1,000 operations
---|---
Before (Jan-Jun) | 14
After (Jul-Dec) | 12

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the team's claim?
choices: Staff reported that the new protocol took longer to complete.
Two other hospitals adopted a similar protocol the same year.
Infection rates fell from 14 to 12 per 1,000 operations, a change of 2 that is within the ward's normal year-to-year variation.
The hospital performed more operations after July than before.
items.explanation: A two-per-thousand change inside normal variation gives no evidence of an effect, which undercuts the claim of reduction.
items.skill_note: The claim is causal; small movements within baseline noise cannot support it.

items.passage: Engineers argue that the durability of Roman harbor concrete comes from a reaction between volcanic ash and seawater, which grows crystals that seal cracks.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the engineers' argument?
choices: Modern concrete made with the same volcanic ash and cured in seawater sealed a hairline crack within a month, while identical mixes without the ash widened the crack.
Volcanic ash was widely traded across the Mediterranean.
Roman harbor concrete contains aggregate from at least four different quarries.
The harbor structures have survived eighteen centuries of wave action.
items.explanation: A controlled comparison in which ash alone produces self-sealing identifies the reaction as the cause of durability.
items.skill_note: Long survival is the phenomenon to be explained, not evidence for a particular explanation.

items.passage: A government credits its 2018 corporate tax cut with a surge in business investment that began the following year, pointing to a nineteen percent rise in machinery purchases.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the government's claim?
choices: Investment in the retail sector grew faster than in manufacturing.
A neighboring country with no tax change recorded the same proportional investment surge in the same two years, driven by a global fall in the price of machinery.
Business associations had lobbied for the cut for a decade.
The tax cut reduced revenue by 40 billion dollars over three years.
items.explanation: An identical surge where the policy did not exist attributes the investment to a common external cause.
items.skill_note: Revenue loss measures cost, not causation.

items.passage: A soil scientist proposes that adding crushed basalt to farmland increases the amount of carbon stored in the soil, because the rock weathers and captures carbon dioxide as carbonate minerals.
items.stem:
The trial compared plots on the same farm and soil type.

Plot treatment | Change in soil carbon over 4 years (t/ha)
---|---
No basalt | 0.3
Basalt applied | 2.4

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the proposal?
choices: Treated plots produced slightly higher wheat yields.
Basalt application raised soil pH by 0.4 units.
The basalt was obtained from a quarry 60 kilometers away.
Basalt-treated plots gained 2.4  t/ha of soil carbon against 0.3  t/ha in untreated plots, and carbonate minerals were found only in the treated plots.
items.explanation: A sevenfold carbon gain together with carbonate minerals appearing only where basalt was added supports the weathering mechanism.
items.skill_note: A pH change is a plausible side effect; it does not show carbon was captured as carbonate.

items.passage: A climatologist argues that the exceptionally cold summer of 1816 in the northern hemisphere was caused by the eruption of Mount Tambora the previous year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the climatologist's argument?
choices: Ice cores from both Greenland and Antarctica contain a sulfate layer dated to 1815 whose mass matches Tambora's estimated output, and climate models forced with that sulfate reproduce the observed summer cooling.
Contemporary newspaper accounts describe frost in June and July.
Tambora's eruption killed tens of thousands of people locally.
Several other volcanoes erupted in the same decade.
items.explanation: Dated sulfate of the right magnitude plus a model that reproduces the cooling links this eruption to this summer.
items.skill_note: Frost reports establish the cold but not its cause.

items.passage: A cardiologist claims that a workplace stair-climbing program lowers blood pressure among sedentary office workers, citing a twelve-week trial in four buildings where employees had previously taken the lift.
items.stem:
Offices were randomly assigned to the program or to a waiting list.

Group | Mean fall in systolic pressure (mmHg)
---|---
Waiting list | 1
Program | 2

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Participants climbed an average of six flights a day.
The program ran for twelve weeks during working hours.
Pressure fell 2 mmHg in the program group against 1 mmHg on the waiting list, a difference smaller than the monitor's own error of 4 mmHg.
items.explanation: A one-millimeter difference inside measurement error gives no support for a blood-pressure effect.
items.skill_note: That participants climbed stairs confirms the intervention happened, not that it worked.

items.passage: A paleographer argues that two volumes of a chronicle, though now held in different libraries, were copied in the same scriptorium within a few years of each other.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the paleographer's argument?
choices: Both volumes were donated to their libraries in the eighteenth century.
The two volumes share a distinctive ink recipe and the same scribal hand, and their parchment comes from animals slaughtered in the same season.
The two libraries are four hundred kilometers apart.
The chronicle survives in seven other copies.
items.explanation: Shared ink, hand, and parchment batch are production evidence tying the volumes to one workshop and moment.
items.skill_note: Provenance and distance describe later history, not where the books were made.

items.passage: A school district claims that its new small-group tutoring program raised reading scores for struggling third graders, and cites a gain of nine points in the tutored group.
items.stem:
Tutored and untutored struggling readers appear in the table.

Group | Mean gain in reading score (points)
---|---
Tutored | 62
Not tutored | 60

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the district's claim?
choices: Tutors received twelve hours of training before the term began.
Tutoring was delivered in groups of four for thirty minutes a day.
Tutored students gained 62 points against 60 for untutored students, a difference of 2 inside the test's five-point margin of error.
The district spent 400,000 dollars on the program.
items.explanation: A two-point difference inside the test's error margin cannot support a claim of a nine-point program effect.
items.skill_note: Program details and cost describe implementation, not impact.

items.passage: A glaciologist argues that a Greenland ice sheet margin had already retreated several kilometers inland before 1900, earlier than most reconstructions assume.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the glaciologist's argument?
choices: Moss buried under the current ice margin yields a radiocarbon age of 1,650 years, and the trimline it marks lies four kilometers inside the position shown on an 1880 survey.
The ice sheet has lost mass in every decade since 1970.
Satellite measurements since 1979 show accelerating retreat.
The margin is currently retreating by about thirty meters a year.
items.explanation: Dated buried vegetation and a trimline inside the 1880 position establish that retreat had occurred before that survey.
items.skill_note: Modern acceleration says nothing about the nineteenth-century position.

items.passage: A hospital's operations team claims that a new scheduling system reduced patient waiting times in its emergency department by a third.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The system cost 2.4 million dollars and required new software licenses.
The department sees about 300 patients a day.
Nurses received three days of training on the system.
Waiting times were measured only at the smaller of two campuses, where the new system was installed six months earlier, and the larger campus recorded a nine percent increase over the same period.
items.explanation: A gain at one site with a loss at the other, measured over different periods, does not support a department-wide reduction.
items.skill_note: Cost and training are implementation facts, not evidence about waiting times.

items.passage: A climatologist argues that the crop failures of 1816 in New England were caused by the eruption of Mount Tambora, which injected sulfate into the stratosphere the previous year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the climatologist's argument?
choices: Several eruptions occurred in Indonesia during the 1810s.
Tree rings across New England show the coldest June-to-August growth of the century in 1816, and an Antarctic ice core records a sulfate spike dated to 1815 at the layer corresponding to that year.
Tambora's eruption was heard 2,000 kilometers away.
Newspapers in 1816 reported frost in every month of the summer.
items.explanation: Coincident tree-ring cooling and a dated sulfate layer tie the cold summer to the volcanic aerosol.
items.skill_note: Frost reports establish the event but not the mechanism; several contemporaneous eruptions complicate an attribution made without the sulfate date.

items.passage: A researcher hypothesizes that a vitamin D supplement reduces fractures in older adults living at northern latitudes, where winter sunlight is insufficient for skin synthesis.
items.stem:
Participants were randomly assigned to supplement or placebo and followed for five years.

Group | Fractures per 1,000 person-years
---|---
Placebo | 28
Supplement | 27

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis?
choices: Adherence to the supplement was 84 percent.
Blood levels of vitamin D rose substantially in the supplement group.
Fracture rates were 27 per 1,000 person-years on the supplement against 28 on placebo, a difference of 1.
Participants were recruited from four northern countries.
items.explanation: The supplement raised blood levels but produced no meaningful change in fractures, which undercuts the proposed benefit.
items.skill_note: That the supplement was absorbed shows the intervention worked as designed, not that it prevented fractures.

items.passage: A paleographer argues that the main scribe of a ninth-century gospel book, who wrote all two hundred surviving pages, was left-handed rather than right-handed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The scribe's name appears in a colophon at the end.
The letters slant consistently to the left, the pen strokes are heaviest on the right-hand side of each minim, and smudges cluster where a left hand would rest on drying ink.
A later hand added notes in the margins of six pages.
The book was copied on calfskin of unusually high quality.
items.explanation: Slant, stroke weight, and smudge placement are the physical traces a left-handed pen grip leaves.
items.skill_note: A colophon identifies the scribe but says nothing about which hand he used.

items.passage: A geneticist argues that a variant of the hemoglobin gene protects carriers against malaria rather than merely being common in malarial regions by coincidence.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the geneticist's argument?
choices: In a controlled infection study, carriers of the variant developed parasitemia at half the rate of non-carriers, and the variant's frequency rises with historical malaria prevalence across forty populations.
The variant alters the shape of red blood cells under low oxygen.
Sequencing has identified more than 200 hemoglobin variants.
The variant is more common in equatorial Africa than in northern Europe.
items.explanation: A measured protective effect under controlled exposure, plus a dose-response with malaria history, establishes protection rather than coincidence.
items.skill_note: Cell shape describes a mechanism that could matter without showing any protective outcome.

items.passage: A company claims that its merger with a rival in 2019 produced large efficiency gains, pointing to a twenty percent fall in operating costs per unit between 2018 and 2022.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the company's claim?
choices: The combined company closed two warehouses after the merger.
The rival had been losing market share for five years.
The merger required approval from three competition authorities.
Operating costs per unit had been falling by about five percent a year since 2013, and the decline continued at that rate after the merger with no change in slope.
items.explanation: A pre-existing trend that continues unchanged leaves the merger nothing to explain.
items.skill_note: Closing warehouses shows restructuring happened, not that it caused the cost decline.

items.passage: A limnologist argues that fertilizer runoff from farms, not sewage from the town on the shore, is driving the algal blooms that now close the lake each August.
items.stem:
Bloom days for two reaches of the lake appear in the table.

Lake reach | Bloom days per summer (days)
---|---
Upstream of farms | 38
Downstream of farms | 40

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the argument?
choices: The lake's phosphorus concentration has risen since 1990.
Blue-green algae produce toxins that harm fish.
The upstream reach, which receives no farm runoff, recorded 38 bloom days against 40 downstream.
items.explanation: Blooms of nearly the same duration where no farm runoff enters indicate that something other than fertilizer is driving them.
items.skill_note: Rising phosphorus is consistent with either source and does not separate them.

items.passage: A utility argues that its rooftop solar program reduced afternoon demand on the grid, easing the strain that peaks on hot days.
items.stem:
Rooftop installations grew from 4,000 to 61,000 between the two years.

Year | Mean 4 p.m. demand (MW)
---|---
2015 | 1000
2024 | 820

Which finding, if true, would most directly support the utility's argument?
choices: Total annual electricity sales were flat over the period.
Mean 4 p.m. demand fell from 1000 to 820  MW while the number of installations grew fifteenfold and summer temperatures were comparable.
Three commercial solar farms were built in the same years.
The program offered a 30 percent rebate on installation.
items.explanation: A 180 MW fall at the peak hour, with comparable weather and a fifteenfold increase in rooftop capacity, supports the claimed effect.
items.skill_note: Flat annual sales do not show what happened at the peak hour.

items.passage: A health ministry claims that its 2015 anti-smoking campaign, which ran on television for six months, reduced adult smoking prevalence by two percentage points.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The campaign included graphic warning labels and a television spot.
The ministry spent 22 million dollars on the campaign.
Prevalence had been falling by about 0.8 percentage points a year since 2005, and it continued to fall by 0.8 points a year after the campaign began.
Smoking among teenagers fell faster than among adults.
items.explanation: An unchanged rate of decline across the campaign's start leaves no detectable effect for the campaign.
items.skill_note: Spending and content describe the campaign, not its impact.

items.passage: A historian argues that a corpus of Linear A tablets was written right to left, though the direction is disputed.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The script has never been deciphered.
The tablets were found in a storeroom with clay sealings.
Similar signs appear on pottery from the same period.
Repeated sign groups begin at the right edge of the tablet, the left edges are worn smooth where a hand would rest, and overlapping strokes show each sign cut before the one to its right.
items.explanation: Stroke overlap is the decisive physical evidence: signs cut before the one to their right fix the direction.
items.skill_note: Lack of decipherment is irrelevant to the direction the signs were written.

items.passage: A liturgical historian argues that a twelfth-century psalter was copied for use at Durham Cathedral rather than at an abbey in the south, despite its southern-style script.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
choices: The calendar of saints in the psalter includes three feasts observed only at Durham, and the litany names a local hermit whose cult never spread beyond the diocese.
The psalter's script resembles that of southern scriptoria.
The book was purchased by a collector in 1780.
The psalter contains 150 psalms and eight canticles.
items.explanation: A calendar with Durham-only feasts and a purely local saint identifies the use the book was made for, whatever the script looks like.
items.skill_note: Script can travel with a scribe; the calendar has to match the institution that used the book.

items.passage: A geologist argues that a landslide on a steep slope was triggered by a magnitude 6.2 earthquake whose epicenter lay 40 kilometers away.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The landslide blocked a river for eleven days.
The region experiences several earthquakes each decade.
The slope is composed of layered shale and sandstone.
Seismograph records place the earthquake at the moment the slope failed, tree rings show the trees on the slide were killed that spring, and the slope had shown no movement in twenty years of survey.
items.explanation: Exact timing, a dated kill event, and a previously stable slope tie the failure to that earthquake.
items.skill_note: Regional seismicity shows earthquakes are common, not that this one caused the slide.

items.passage: A numismatist argues that a hoard of silver coins found in a Welsh field was minted locally rather than imported from the continent.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The field had been plowed for at least a century.
Three of the coins were struck from the same die as coins in a securely provenanced local hoard, and their silver matches the trace-element signature of a nearby mine.
Coins of this type circulate widely in northern Europe.
The hoard contained 214 coins in total.
items.explanation: A shared die proves a common mint, and the metal signature ties the silver to a local source.
items.skill_note: Wide circulation shows the type traveled; it does not show where these coins were struck.

items.passage: A management researcher hypothesizes that larger research teams produce less innovative work per person than smaller teams, because coordination costs grow faster than ideas.
items.stem:
Novelty was scored on a 0-10 scale by blinded reviewers.

Team size | Novelty score per author
---|---
2-4 authors | 6.1
10+ authors | 6.3

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the hypothesis?
choices: Large teams scored 6.3 per author against 6.1 for small teams, a difference of 0.2 in the opposite direction from the hypothesis.
Small teams published more papers in total.
Novelty scores were normally distributed within each group.
Large teams were more common in physics than in history.
items.explanation: A slightly higher per-author novelty in large teams contradicts the predicted decline, however small the margin.
items.skill_note: Total output is a different measure from novelty per person.

items.passage: An astronomer argues that a comet observed in 2023 is the same object recorded in 1642, not a new comet.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Comets are known to lose material at each perihelion passage.
The 1642 comet was recorded by observers in China and Europe.
The 2023 orbit, calculated from forty observations, matches the 1642 orbit to within the historical measurement error, including the same close approach to Jupiter in both apparitions.
The 2023 comet was visible to the naked eye for six weeks.
items.explanation: An orbital match, including the same planetary encounter, identifies the object rather than merely suggesting a resemblance.
items.skill_note: Visibility and historical records show the comet was seen, not that it was the same body.

items.passage: A park service argues that reintroducing wolves in 1995 restored streamside willows by reducing the elk browsing that had stripped new growth for decades.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the argument?
choices: Willow cover had begun to increase in 1988, seven years before the wolves arrived, and browsing intensity measured on exclosures remained unchanged after reintroduction.
Wolves were transplanted from Canada in two winters.
Elk numbers fell by a third after the wolves returned.
Beaver activity increased along two of the monitored streams.
items.explanation: Recovery that predates the wolves, with browsing unchanged, breaks the causal chain the argument requires.
items.skill_note: A falling elk count is consistent with the story but does not show willows responded.

items.passage: A glaciologist argues that a valley glacier advanced several kilometers during the nineteenth century, before the retreat that continues today.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Local records mention a poor harvest in 1832.
The valley is fed by a high-altitude snowfield.
The glacier has retreated four kilometers since 1900.
A moraine six kilometers downvalley contains logs buried by ice, radiocarbon dated to 1830-1850, and the same moraine truncates a farm wall built in 1790.
items.explanation: Dated buried wood inside a moraine that cuts a 1790 wall places the advance in the nineteenth century.
items.skill_note: Twentieth-century retreat shows the glacier is shrinking now, not that it grew earlier.

items.passage: A zooarchaeologist argues that a coastal hunting camp, occupied for perhaps a century, was used during the winter months rather than in the summer fishing season.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Stone tools at the site were made from local flint.
The camp lies 400 meters from the present shoreline.

Oxygen isotope profiles in the growth layers of recovered seal teeth record a winter birth and a first-year growth pattern that ends in winter, and the site's bird bones are all of species present only in winter.
The site was excavated over three seasons.
items.explanation: Tooth growth increments and winter-only bird species both fix the season of occupation.
items.skill_note: Distance to the shore reflects later coastal change, not the season of use.

items.passage: A cardiology group claims that high-dose omega-3 supplements reduce the risk of atrial fibrillation in older adults, who face rising risk of the condition.
items.stem:
Participants were randomized to high-dose omega-3 or placebo.

Group | New atrial fibrillation per 1,000 person-years
---|---
Placebo | 24
Omega-3 | 31

Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: The dose was 1.8 grams a day.
New cases were 31 per 1,000 person-years on omega-3 against 24 on placebo, a difference of 7 in the direction opposite to the claim.
Participants were followed for a median of five years.
The supplement lowered triglycerides by 20 percent.
items.explanation: A higher incidence in the treated group directly contradicts a claimed reduction.
items.skill_note: Lower triglycerides is a different outcome and does not rescue the claim about rhythm.

items.passage: A climate scientist argues that the eruption of an Icelandic volcano in 1783, the largest of the millennium, cooled Europe for two years afterward.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The eruption produced lava flows that destroyed farms.
Contemporary accounts describe a dry fog across Europe that summer.
Ice cores record a sulfate layer in 1783 at four times the usual volcanic background, and tree rings from Germany and Scotland show the two coldest summers of the century in 1783 and 1784.
Iceland lost most of its livestock to fluorine poisoning.
items.explanation: A dated sulfate spike matched to two years of exceptional cold links the eruption to the cooling.
items.skill_note: A dry fog is consistent with the eruption but does not measure temperature or timing.

items.passage: A pharmacologist proposes that a new compound lowers blood pressure by blocking a receptor in the kidney rather than by relaxing blood vessels directly. In mice engineered to lack that receptor, the compound has no effect on pressure.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the pharmacologist's proposal?
choices: In normal mice, the compound binds the kidney receptor at the same dose that lowers pressure, and a second compound that blocks the receptor without relaxing vessels has the same effect.
The compound lowered pressure in rats as well as mice.
The compound has a half-life of about six hours in mice.
The compound is excreted unchanged in the urine within six hours.
items.explanation: Binding at the effective dose plus an independent receptor blocker reproducing the effect ties the pressure drop to that receptor specifically.
items.skill_note: A result in a second species shows generality, not mechanism.

items.passage: A historian argues that the famine of 1846 in a coastal province was caused by the failure of the potato harvest rather than by the government's decision to continue exporting grain.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the historian's argument?
choices: The potato blight reached the province two weeks earlier than expected.
The government received warnings about the harvest in August.
Grain prices in the province doubled between 1845 and 1846.
Provinces that harvested the same failed crop but banned grain exports recorded a quarter of the mortality, with the difference concentrated among landless laborers.
items.explanation: If banning exports sharply reduced mortality under the same harvest failure, export policy was a cause the historian's account omits.
items.skill_note: Price movements are consistent with either explanation and do not discriminate between them.

items.passage: A linguist argues that the ancestors of a language family domesticated horses, because the reconstructed proto-language has a word for wheel and for harness that is shared across all its branches.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguist's argument?
choices: The word for horse differs sharply among the branches.

The reconstructed words refer to spoke-wheeled vehicles and to a horse collar, and the earliest physical examples of both appear in the region the linguist identifies, dated to the period of the proposed expansion.
Several branches borrowed metalworking terms from unrelated neighbors.
The family includes twelve modern languages spoken across two continents.
items.explanation: Specific referents plus matching archaeological dates tie the vocabulary to the technology and the place, which is what the argument needs.
items.skill_note: Geographic spread shows the family expanded; it does not show what its speakers did.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new talking therapy halves relapse rates in depression compared with usual care, and concludes that the therapy's specific techniques are responsible.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that conclusion?
choices: Relapse was assessed by interviewers unaware of group assignment.
The therapy was delivered by clinicians with an average of nine years' experience.
Participants in the therapy arm attended 78 percent of sessions.
The comparison group received far fewer clinical contact hours, and a second arm given the same number of hours of nonspecific support had relapse rates identical to the therapy arm.
items.explanation: If equal contact hours without the techniques produce the same result, the benefit comes from attention, not from the specific techniques.
items.skill_note: Blinded assessment and attendance improve the study's quality without addressing what caused the benefit.

items.passage: A museum replaced the fluorescent bulbs in its textile gallery with LEDs, expecting the rate at which dyed fabrics fade to fall by half. After two years, the curators reported that the fading rate was unchanged.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly explain the failure rather than the expectation?
choices: The gallery's temperature is held constant at 20 degrees.
The new fixtures emit almost no ultraviolet light, but the fading is driven by visible blue light, which the LEDs produce at nearly the same intensity as the old bulbs.
The LEDs were more expensive to purchase than the fluorescents they replaced.
Visitors spend an average of nine minutes in the gallery.
items.explanation: Fading driven by blue light, which the new fixtures did not reduce, accounts for the unchanged rate without contradicting the physics.
items.skill_note: Cost and temperature are irrelevant to why the fading rate stayed the same.

items.passage: A forest pathologist argues that a bark beetle is killing stands of pine not by girdling the trees but by carrying a fungus that blocks their water-conducting tissue.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the pathologist's argument?
choices: Trees injected with a fungicide before beetles were introduced survived at four times the rate of untreated trees, though both groups were attacked equally, and the fungus was recovered from the sapwood of every dead tree.
Beetle populations increase in years following mild winters.
Several species of pine are affected across the region.
Dead trees show galleries carved beneath the bark.
items.explanation: Fungicide protection with equal beetle attack isolates the fungus, rather than the physical wounding, as the lethal agent.
items.skill_note: Galleries prove the beetles were present; they do not show what killed the trees.

items.passage: A conservator argues that the blue in a wall painting is Egyptian blue rather than a modern synthetic pigment, despite the painting's having been restored in 1932.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the conservator's argument?
choices: A restorer's notebook from 1932 mentions repairing the sky.
The blue appears in the sky, the drapery, and the border.
The blue grains contain cuprorivaite crystals with a calcium-to-copper ratio matching Egyptian blue made before 1000 CE, and no grains show the spherical shape produced by modern milling.
The painting was cleaned twice in the twentieth century.
items.explanation: Crystal chemistry and grain shape identify the pigment's manufacture, which is what distinguishes an ancient from a modern blue.
items.skill_note: Restoration records show the area was touched, not what pigment was used.

items.passage: A volcanologist argues that a massive eruption in 1600 BCE, not one in 1500 BCE, produced the ash layer found across the eastern Mediterranean.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Ice cores from Greenland contain a sulfate spike somewhere in that century.
The ash layer sits directly beneath a tree-ring frost marker dated to 1598 BCE, and radiocarbon dates on olive branches buried by the eruption cluster between 1610 and 1590 BCE.
Ash from the eruption has been found in Egypt and Turkey.
The eruption was one of the largest of the Holocene.
items.explanation: A frost marker immediately above the ash plus a tight radiocarbon range places the eruption within a decade of 1600 BCE.
items.skill_note: A sulfate spike 'somewhere in that century' cannot separate 1600 from 1500.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new drug reduced mortality in patients with severe infections, and the authors recommend it as standard care.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the recommendation?
choices: The drug was administered intravenously for seven days.
The trial took place in eleven hospitals across three countries.
Patients in both arms received the same supportive care.
The trial stopped after 120 of a planned 600 patients, the mortality difference was two percentage points, and twice as many treated patients withdrew because of kidney injury.
items.explanation: A small difference in a truncated trial, with more harm-driven withdrawals, is too fragile to support a standard-of-care recommendation.
items.skill_note: Multinational recruitment improves generalizability; it does not repair a stopped trial with a tiny effect.

items.passage: A conservator argues that a blue pigment on a Roman wall in Pompeii was applied in antiquity and is not a later repaint.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: The pigment particles are embedded in cracks that formed when the plaster cured in antiquity, and a fragment of the same plaster overlaying the blue carries a dateable mortar from the original construction.
Roman painters are known to have used several blue minerals.
The wall was exposed by excavation in 1876.
The blue matches pigments used elsewhere in the same room.
items.explanation: Pigment inside ancient curing cracks can only have been there before those cracks formed, which rules out repainting.
items.skill_note: A match to nearby pigment shows consistency, not priority in time.

items.passage: A district reports that schools adopting a new reading program saw comprehension scores rise by eight points in one year, and concludes the program works.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that conclusion?
choices: Teachers received coaching visits every two weeks.
The district spent 1.1 million dollars on materials.
The schools that adopted the program were selected because their scores had been falling unusually fast, and scores in those schools rebounded to their previous level rather than exceeding it.
The program required ninety minutes of daily instruction.
items.explanation: Regression from an unusually low baseline explains the gain without any effect of the program.
items.skill_note: Coaching and time on task show fidelity of implementation, not effect.

items.passage: A trial reports that a new vaccine reduced symptomatic infections by 70 percent, and the authors suggest it will substantially reduce transmission in the community.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken that suggestion?
choices: The trial enrolled 28,000 participants across four countries.
Viral loads in the noses of vaccinated participants who nevertheless became infected were as high as those in unvaccinated participants, and those participants reported mild or no symptoms.
The vaccine was given in two doses three weeks apart.
Protection against severe disease was over 90 percent.
items.explanation: Equal viral loads among vaccinated cases imply they can still transmit, which undercuts a community-level effect.
items.skill_note: Protection against severe disease is compatible with continued transmission and does not weaken the suggestion.

items.passage: A consumer group claims that a supermarket merger in 2018, which combined two chains with overlapping stores in six cities, lowered prices for shoppers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Prices fell across the whole region over the same years as wholesale food costs dropped, and stores in areas where the merger reduced competition by more than half fell less than the regional average.
The merger was reviewed by a national regulator.
The two chains had overlapped in six cities.
The merged chain closed twelve stores in rural areas.
items.explanation: A regional cost decline plus smaller declines where competition was reduced indicates the merger did not lower prices.
items.skill_note: Store closures show consolidation happened, not what it did to prices.

items.passage: A linguist argues that a set of words entered an island language from Latin through a neighboring trading language rather than directly from Latin.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the argument?
choices: Latin was the administrative language of the nearest province.
The words all relate to commerce and shipping.
The island was visited by Roman ships in the first century.
The words show sound changes characteristic of the trading language but absent from Latin, and include a suffix that Latin did not possess but the trading language did.
items.explanation: Sound changes and morphology that match the intermediary, not the source, identify the route of borrowing.
items.skill_note: Commerce vocabulary fits the meaning but not the pathway.

items.passage: A city claims that its 2019 housing-first policy, which gave apartments and case management to several hundred people, reduced street homelessness by 40 percent in two years.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the claim?
choices: Two neighboring cities adopted similar policies in 2020.
The policy provided 900 apartments with case management.

The city changed its street count in 2019 from a single-night census to a week-long average that counts people in shelters as housed, and the 2018 figure was revised upward by a third before the comparison was published.
The city's shelter capacity grew by 300 beds.
items.explanation: A changed counting method and a revised baseline mean the 40 percent drop may be an artifact of measurement.
items.skill_note: New apartments show the policy was implemented, not that homelessness fell.
